prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "JD.com, Inc." (ticker JD), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "JD", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: JD.com, Inc.
markets: China online retail (electronics, appliances, general merchandise, groceries)
Logistics and supply chain services (JD Logistics)
Food delivery and instant retail (JD Takeaway, launched 2025)
International e-commerce (Joybuy in Europe, Ceconomy/MediaMarkt deal)
Industrial supply chain and B2B procurement (JD Industrials)

mission.statement: Powered by technology for a more productive and sustainable world
mission.plain: JD wants to use technology to make shopping and supply chains work better and waste less.

about.plain: JD.com is one of China's biggest online shops. Unlike most rivals, it buys and stocks a lot of the goods itself and delivers them with its own trucks, warehouses and couriers, often on the same or next day. It is especially known for selling real, not fake, phones, computers and home appliances. It also runs a delivery company, an online pharmacy, and since 2025 a food delivery service.
about.customers: Hundreds of millions of Chinese shoppers, plus brands, merchants and businesses that sell on JD or use its delivery network.
about.everyday: It is like China's version of Amazon: you order a phone or a fridge on the app and a JD courier brings it to your door, often the same day.

money.part: Selling products directly (electronics, appliances, groceries, general goods)
money.plain: goods JD buys and resells online
warehousing and delivery for JD and other companies (JD Logistics)
commissions and ads paid by third-party sellers
JD Takeaway food delivery, Jingxi, overseas Joybuy
online and store retail in Europe

money.part: Robotics, autonomous delivery and AI models
money.plain: self-driving delivery vehicles, warehouse robots, JoyAI models

result.summary: JD has a real but narrow advantage: a nationwide self-built logistics network and a reputation for genuine goods and fast delivery that took nearly two decades and hundreds of billions of yuan to build. That advantage is strongest in electronics and appliances, but it has not given JD pricing power, because Alibaba, PDD and Douyin compete hard on price and JD's net margin was only 1.5% in 2025 after heavy food-delivery losses.

pricingPower.evidence: JD's gross margin rose only from 14.6% in 2020 to 16.0% in 2025 while it ran repeated low-price campaigns and government trade-in subsidies; revenue fell 2.9% year on year in Q2 2026 when subsidies faded, showing volumes depend on price.

moats.evidence: JD is widely trusted in China for authentic electronics and appliances and fast delivery, which matters in a market with counterfeit risk, but the brand does not let it charge higher prices.
Shoppers can switch between JD, Taobao, PDD and Douyin with a tap; the JD PLUS membership adds only mild stickiness.
Its marketplace has some two-sided effects, but JD is mainly a first-party retailer and its third-party marketplace is smaller than Alibaba's or PDD's.

With RMB1.31 trillion of 2025 revenue and RMB217 billion of logistics segment revenue, JD gets supplier terms and per-parcel delivery costs few rivals can match, though PDD reaches low prices with an asset-light model.
China e-commerce is not a natural monopoly; several well-funded platforms coexist and new entrants such as Douyin have taken share.
JD's asset-heavy first-party model is well known and rivals have chosen not to copy it rather than being unable to.
Two decades of supply-chain operation give JD an inventory turnover and same/next-day delivery capability that peers have found hard and costly to replicate.
Its warehouse network and delivery workforce are valuable, but they are owned assets that a determined rival could build over time, not exclusive rights.

customers.evidence: JD is known for genuine goods and reliable after-sales service, and its JD PLUS paid membership has tens of millions of members, but customer loyalty is price-sensitive and JD stopped disclosing annual active customer numbers after 2022.

talent.evidence: JD offers above-average pay and in 2025 raised pay and social-insurance coverage for couriers and riders, but Chinese internet workplaces have a reputation for long hours and JD does not top major employer rankings.

product.evidence: Its logistics speed (same or next day in most of China) and authenticity are best in class for electronics and appliances, but its app and range are not clearly superior to Taobao/Tmall or PDD for general goods and low prices.

competitors.name: Alibaba Group (Taobao, Tmall)
competitors.note: China online retail, instant retail and food delivery (Taobao Instant Commerce, Ele.me)

competitors.name: PDD Holdings (Pinduoduo, Temu)
competitors.note: Value-focused China e-commerce, groceries and cross-border

competitors.name: Meituan
competitors.note: Food delivery and instant retail versus JD Takeaway and JD's instant delivery

competitors.name: SF Holding
competitors.note: Express delivery and supply-chain logistics versus JD Logistics

competitors.name: Suning.com
competitors.note: Electronics and appliance retail in China

competitors.note: European e-commerce versus Joybuy, and global logistics

competitors.name: Walmart (incl. Sam's Club China)
competitors.note: Grocery and membership retail in China

threats: Food delivery war with Meituan and Alibaba: New Businesses lost RMB46.6 billion in 2025 and RMB9.9 billion in Q2 2026, cutting group operating margin to 0.2% in 2025
Fading Chinese government trade-in subsidies for appliances and electronics, JD's core categories; revenue fell 2.9% in Q2 2026
Price competition from PDD and Douyin's livestream commerce taking share of China online retail
Weak Chinese consumer spending and deflation
Execution risk in Europe (Joybuy launch in March 2026 and the roughly EUR2.2 billion Ceconomy/MediaMarkt takeover)
Chinese regulation (platform pricing rules, courier social-insurance requirements) and US-China tensions including possible ADR delisting pressure

ceo.name: Sandy Ran Xu
ceo.background: Former PwC audit partner for nearly 20 years, CPA in China and the US; JD CFO 2020-2023; Peking University bachelor's in information science and economics. Founder Richard Liu remains chairman.

c1.evidence: China e-commerce is a large but maturing industry and JD is the number two or three player behind Alibaba and PDD, with revenue growth of 13% in 2025 and -2.9% in Q2 2026.

c2.evidence: Customers choose JD for authentic goods and same/next-day delivery from its self-built logistics network, which is costly to copy, but rivals win on price and the advantage has not produced pricing power.

c3.evidence: Almost every Chinese shopper knows JD and it is the default for buying electronics and appliances online, but it is not the overall category leader and is little known outside China.

c4.evidence: JD's mission 'Powered by technology for a more productive and sustainable world' is published but rarely emphasised; founder Richard Liu's public messaging focuses more on quality goods, fair treatment of couriers and fighting competitors.

c6.evidence: “genuine goods, fast delivery, electronics” – the impression is mostly positive among Chinese consumers, tempered by investor views of JD as a low-margin retailer caught in price and food-delivery wars.

c7.evidence: China's online retail market is huge and still growing as a share of retail, but growth has slowed to mid-single digits and is not a strong new secular trend like AI.

c8.evidence: JD has expanded into food delivery (2025), healthcare (JD Health), industrial procurement, logistics for third parties, and Europe via Joybuy (March 2026) and the Ceconomy/MediaMarkt takeover.

m1.evidence: CEO Sandy Xu is an operator and former CFO focused on execution and efficiency; the long-term vision (logistics, food delivery, Europe) is driven mainly by founder-chairman Richard Liu.

m2.evidence: Xu is a professional manager, not a founder, but founder Richard Liu still controls the majority of votes and is personally driving the food-delivery and overseas push.

m4.evidence: JD is unusual among Chinese platforms in giving couriers full social insurance and in 2025 extended coverage to full-time food-delivery riders, though this owes much to Richard Liu.

m5.evidence: JD has a distinctive operations-heavy culture that built in-house logistics, autonomous delivery and warehouse robots, but it is seen more as an operator than a product inventor.

m6.evidence: Sandy Xu's background is accounting and finance (PwC audit partner, JD CFO), not engineering or product.

m7.evidence: There is no public controversy about Sandy Xu's character, but there is little public evidence either way about her personal values beyond running the company.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Sandy Xu at a top university is publicly recorded.

m8b.evidence: Sandy Xu keeps a low public profile; the memorable public personality at JD is founder Richard Liu.

m9.evidence: Under Xu, operating income rose from RMB26.0 billion in 2023 to RMB38.7 billion in 2024, but it fell to RMB2.8 billion in 2025 as food delivery losses mounted, before recovering to RMB4.5 billion in Q2 2026.

m10.evidence: JD has run repeated cost-efficiency drives and manager pay cuts (Richard Liu's 2022 cost reforms), but it also spends heavily on logistics, food delivery subsidies and Europe.

c10.evidence: JD improves daily life for hundreds of millions of people in China with fast, reliable delivery of genuine goods, but its reach outside China is still small.

p2.evidence: Building and running a nationwide same-day logistics network for over a trillion yuan of sales is very hard, though the service itself (retail and delivery) is not uniquely important to the world.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew every year from RMB745.8 billion in 2020 to RMB951.6 billion (2021), RMB1,046.2 billion (2022), RMB1,084.7 billion (2023), RMB1,158.8 billion (2024) and RMB1,309.1 billion (2025).

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 14.6% in 2020 to 16.0% in 2025, but operating margin fell from 1.7% (RMB12.3 billion) to 0.2% (RMB2.8 billion) because of food-delivery losses.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 JD held RMB221.7 billion of cash and short-term investments against RMB69.9 billion of debt and senior notes, with RMB282.4 billion of total equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income went from RMB12.3 billion (2020) to RMB2.8 billion (2025) and operating cash flow from RMB42.5 billion to RMB19.0 billion, after peaking in 2023-2024.

v1.evidence: For electronics and appliances JD is many shoppers' first choice because goods are genuine and arrive fast with good after-sales service, but for general goods and lowest prices Taobao or PDD are often preferred.

v2.evidence: JD is not ranked near the top of major employer rankings; it is respected for courier benefits but known for demanding hours.

c5.evidence: If JD disappeared, Chinese shoppers would miss its reliable same-day delivery and trusted electronics, and hundreds of thousands of couriers would lose comparatively well-protected jobs, though rivals could cover most needs.
